claims.text: In FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy-alloy coatings, wear performance is governed by the temperature-dependent evolution of lattice disorder and dislocation density.
Up to 600 K, a moderate reduction in dislocation density increases the elastic modulus and maintains wear resistance.
Above approximately 900 K, lattice disorder increases rapidly, as indicated by an increased HCP atom fraction.
Above approximately 900 K, dislocation density drops significantly.
The increased lattice disorder and reduced dislocation density above 900 K cause lattice softening and decreased hardness.
High-temperature lattice softening changes the deformation mechanism and increases tangential force and friction coefficient.
The modeled initial state is a 21 Å FeNiCrCoCu coating adhered to a 100 Å × 100 Å × 55 Å single-crystal Cu matrix.
The modeled coating and Cu matrix initially have FCC structures with [100], [010], and [001] orientations.
The controlled intervention is temperature variation among 300, 600, 900, and 1200 K during nanoindentation and friction simulations.
The virtual indenter is pressed to 30 Å at 10 m/s over 300 ps and unloaded at the same speed over 300 ps.
The simulations use periodic boundaries in X and Y, a contractive boundary in Z, an NVE bulk, a Langevin-thermostatted constant-temperature layer, and a fixed 3.56 Å lattice constant.
The lattice remains ordered and dislocation density remains stable from 300 to 600 K.
From 900 to 1200 K, the system transitions to rapid lattice disorder, increased HCP atom fraction, and significantly reduced dislocation density.
The deformation mechanism shifts from stacking-fault-dominated plasticity to deformation controlled by lattice disorder.
Wear resistance and hardness remain relatively stable through 600 K and decrease sharply above approximately 900 K.
Friction coefficient and tangential force increase with temperature and fluctuate notably above 900 K because of rapid lattice disorder.
At the 300 K baseline, the lattice is ordered and has higher dislocation density and hardness than at high temperature.
A critical temperature near 900 K marks the onset of a pronounced decrease in wear resistance.
The exact transition temperature and magnitude of property changes may depend on alloy composition and testing conditions.

contradictions.description: The structural mediator describes dislocation density as stable throughout 300–600 K, whereas the hypothesis and mechanism require a moderate dislocation-density reduction at 600 K that increases elastic modulus.
